sections.subtitle: ASCII table
sections.description:
A computer understands only two states: on and off, represented by the binary digits 1 and 0. To bridge the gap between this binary world and human-readable text, a standardized mapping system was created. This system is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, or ASCII.

The Purpose and Function of ASCII
ASCII serves as a universal translator between humans and machines. It assigns a unique numerical code to every character on a standard keyboard, including letters, digits, punctuation, and special control commands. This ensures that when you press the 'A' key on your keyboard, it is consistently stored and transmitted as the number 65 inside the computer, regardless of the computer's make or model. This standardization is crucial for reliable data storage, processing, and communication between different systems.

The Structure of the ASCII Table
The original ASCII standard uses 7 bits, which allows for 128 unique codes, numbered from 0 to 127. These codes are logically divided into two main groups.

The first 32 codes, from 0 to 31, are designated as Control Characters. These are non-printable commands originally designed to control hardware devices like teletype printers and terminals. For example, code 10 represents a Line Feed, which moves the cursor down, and code 13 represents a Carriage Return, which returns the cursor to the beginning of the line. Code 7 triggers an audible bell sound.

Code 32 is the Space character, which is printable but invisible.

The remaining codes, from 33 to 126, are the Printable Characters. This segment contains the familiar set of characters used in everyday computing.

Codes 48 to 57 represent the digits 0 through 9.
Codes 65 to 90 represent the uppercase Latin letters A through Z.
Codes 97 to 122 represent the lowercase Latin letters a through z.

The rest of the codes are filled with punctuation marks and common mathematical and typographical symbols.

The final code, 127, represents the DELETE control character.

Extended ASCII: Beyond 127
The original 7-bit ASCII was soon extended to 8 bits, or one byte, in various proprietary and standardized ways. This allowed for an additional 128 codes, from 128 to 255. This upper range, often called Extended ASCII, was used to represent special characters, accented letters for non-English languages, and drawing symbols. Unlike the standard 0-127 range, the meanings of codes 128-255 were not universally consistent and depended on the specific character encoding used, such as ISO-8859-1 or the Windows-1252 code page.

The Practical Benefits of ASCII Knowledge
Understanding ASCII provides a deeper insight into how computers operate. For programmers, it is essential for tasks involving character manipulation, string processing, and low-level data encoding. It explains why converting a lowercase letter to uppercase simply involves subtracting 32 from its ASCII value, and it is the foundational layer upon which modern, comprehensive encoding systems like Unicode are built.

In summary, the ASCII table is more than a historical artifact; it is the fundamental dictionary that defines how text is represented in the digital realm. Every piece of text in a program, every message sent over a network, and every document stored on a disk relies on the principles established by this simple yet powerful encoding standard.

SubArray or SubSegment
sections.description:
SubArray or SubSegment: A continuous portion or contiguous sequence 
                        within an array and in order.


let Example arr [] = {1,2,3,4,5}

Subarray: 

{}           an empty array is a subarray
{1,2}        contiguous part
{2,3}        contiguous part
{1,2,3,4,5}  main arr itself as a subarray
{2}          single element 

Not Subarray:

{2,4}  present in the array but not contiguous (next to each other)
{5,4}  order is not the same as the main array



Non-Empty subArray = n* (n+1)/2

sections.subtitle: Things to know about  Subarray or Subsegment
sections.description:
• We can use curly brackets {} or square brackets [] to denote arrays.
• Should be a contiguous subsequence of the parent array. 
  As a result, {1, 1} is not a valid subarray of the array {1, 2, 1}. 
  Since {2} in the middle is skipped, it is not a contiguous subsequence
  anymore.
• The full array itself is a subarray of itself.
• An empty array is a subarray of any array.
• Order of elements in the subarray should be the same as in the array.
   As a result, {2, 1, 1} is not a subarray of {1, 2, 1}.

sections.subtitle: Substring
sections.description:
Substring: A Substring is the same thing as a subarray 
           But in the context of strings.


Non-Empty substring = n* (n+1)/2

sections.subtitle: Things to know about Substring
sections.description:
• A substring is just a subarray that is made up of only characters.
• You can use single ‘ or double quotes " to denote substrings.
• All the rules mentioned for subarrays also apply to substrings.

sections.subtitle: SubSequence
sections.description:
SubSequence: May not be contiguous, but maintain the relative order.


For instance. let, arr [] = {1,2,3,4,5}

Subsequence: 
            {2,3,4} (valid cause in order)
            {2,4}   (valid cause in order)
            {1,2,5} (valid cause in order)

Not sa ubsequence:

{5,4}      (not following order (4 is before 5) )
{1,2,5,3}  (not following order (3 is before 5) )

Non-Empty SubSequence: 2^n - 1

sections.subtitle: SubSet
sections.description:
SubSet: May not be contiguous and may not be in order 
         (duplicate not acceptable). A set is a subset of 
         another set if all its elements are contained 
         by that set.

This means neither contiguity nor ordering of elements matters.

Number of subsets  = 2^n 


For instance, the subsets of the set  --->>  {1, 2, 3} 

All subsets would be: ----->>  
  
Length 1   Length 2    Length 3    Length 0
{1},       {1, 2},
{2},       {1, 3},
{3}        {2, 3},     {1, 2, 3}   {} or ∅
 
Here n is 3 --> 2^3 = 8
Total = 8

sections.subtitle: Things to know about Subset
sections.description:
• Subsets do not need to be contiguous. {1, 3} is a perfectly valid subset.
• Subsets do not need to preserve element order. As a result, both {1, 2} 
  and {2, 1} represent the same subset. While listing the subsets of the set, 
  you can either write {1, 2} or {2, 1}, and it does not matter. But you cannot
  list both at the same time since they are the same thing.

• Note on Sets: Unlike arrays, strings, and sequences, sets do not allow
                duplicate elements. As a result, {1, 2, 1} would not be a valid set.

title: Multiple ways to get vaule of Pi in C

sections.subtitle: Multiple ways to get vaule of Pi in C & C++
sections.description:
In C programming, the value of Pi (approximately 3.14159) can be obtained using several methods:


1. Using the M_PI macro from <math.h>
2. Calculating Pi using trigonometric functions.
3. Defining Pi as a constant.


1. This is the most common and convenient way. You need to include the <math.h> header and, on some systems, define _USE_MATH_DEFINES before including it to ensure these constants are available.

2. You can calculate Pi using functions like asin() or atan() or acos(). 
For example, 
asin(1.0) returns (π/2), so multiplying by 2 gives (π). 
atan(1.0) returns (π/4). So multiplying by 4 gives (π).
acos(-1.0) returns (π).
acos(0.0) returns (π/2). so multiplying by 2 gives (π).


3. You can define Pi as a constant using #define or a const variable.

title: Zero-padding of printf fucntion in C

sections.subtitle: Zero-padding of printf fucntion in C
sections.description:
The format specifier %03d in C's printf function is used to print an integer with a minimum width of 3 digits, padding with leading zeros if the number has fewer than 3 digits.

Here's a breakdown:
%: Introduces a format specifier.
0: This is a flag that indicates zero-padding. If the number of digits is less than the specified width, leading zeros will be used for padding instead of spaces (which is the default behavior if no flag is specified or if a space flag is used).
2: This specifies the minimum field width. The output will occupy at least 3 character positions.
d: This is the conversion specifier for a signed decimal integer.

Explanation of Output:
For num1 (value 5), since it's a single digit and the minimum width is 3 with zero-padding, it prints 005.
For num2 (value 124), it already has 3 digits, so no padding is needed, and it prints 124.
For num3 (value 1236), it exceeds the minimum width of 3, so the entire number 1236 is printed without truncation. The 03 only guarantees a minimum width, not a maximum.
